source.title_on_document: StoryScope: Investigating idiosyncrasies in AI fiction

supplement.where: Appendices A to I inside the PDF (pp. 17-30); code and data at https://github.com/jenna-russell/storyscope
supplement.holds: Dataset statistics (Tables 4-5), human validation of feature extraction (Table 7), memorization audit (Tables 8-9), length audit (Table 10), per-class F1 (Table 11), per-story rarity analysis with SDs and Cohen's d (Appendix G, Table 12, Figure 5), core and fingerprint feature lists (Tables 13-16), prompts (Figures 6-8)

paper_design_summary: The authors take 10,272 human-written short stories from Books3, reverse-engineer a writing prompt for each with Gemini 2.5 Flash, and have five LLMs (Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4) write a story from each prompt, giving 61,608 stories. An LLM pipeline extracts 304 discourse-level narrative features per story; XGBoost classifiers then separate human from AI stories and attribute authorship, and the paper compares how dispersed and how rare human and AI stories are in narrative-feature space. No person receives AI assistance.

studies.label: Parallel corpus of human-written (Books3) and LLM-generated short stories

assignment.what_was_assigned: Nothing is assigned to people. Each human story's reverse-engineered prompt is given to five LLMs; the human story and the five AI stories form the six sources.
assignment.quote: We extract 10,272 human-written stories from Books3 (Presser, 2020). To generate mirrored AI stories, we reverse-engineer writing prompts from each human story

arms.name: Human
arms.description: Published human-written short stories extracted from Books3 anthologies

arms.name: AI (five LLMs)
arms.description: Stories generated from the same prompt by Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, and GPT-5.4

participants.exclusions: No human participants. Corpus: 10,272 prompts / human stories; 61,608 stories in total; models refused 24 stories (p. 3, fn. 8). Test set: 1,384 prompts, 8,301 stories (p. 5); Table 12 and Appendix G use 8,262 test stories (1,377 per source).
participants.who: No participants. Human stories are published short fiction from the Books3 corpus; the number of distinct human authors is not stated. Two annotators validated the feature extraction on 12 stories (p. 19, Table 7); they are not study participants.
participants.quote: We apply STORYSCOPE to a parallel corpus of 10,272 writing prompts, each written by a human author and five LLMs (Claude, DeepSeek, Gemini , GPT, and Kimi), yielding 61,608 stories

ai_tool.name_model: Gemini 3 Flash, Kimi K2.5, DeepSeek V3.2, Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-5.4 (story generation); Gemini 2.5 Flash (prompt extraction); GPT-5.1 (templates, feature discovery); Gemini 3 Flash (feature assignment)
ai_tool.how_used: LLMs write stories on their own from a prompt; no human uses the AI.

task.description: Short stories (mean 4,753 words across the corpus) written to a prompt that names characters, setting, and premise of a published human story, with a target length

outcomes.name: Per-story narrative rarity (mean Euclidean distance to 25 nearest neighbors, as percentile)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean Euclidean distance to a story's k = 25 nearest neighbors in the pooled train+val narrative-feature space, converted to a percentile against the train+val rarity distribution. Also reported: share of stories in the top 1/5/10 percent rarest, and share of prompts where the human story is rarest of six.

contrasts.reported: Mean rarity percentile human 0.71 vs AI 0.49, AUC = 0.73; Cohen's d = 0.83 over 1,377 human and 6,885 AI test stories; SDs 0.227 (human), 0.274 (pooled AI), pooled SD 0.267. Top 10%: 24.7% of human vs 7.1% of AI stories (top 1%: 3.0% vs 0.6%). Human story rarest of six for 57.8% of prompts (vs 16.7% by chance).
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5 'Human narratives are rarer'; p. 22, Appendix G; p. 23, Table 12 and Figure 5

outcomes.name: Dispersion in narrative-feature space (distance to source centroid; 10-nearest-neighbor radius)
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Euclidean distances in the z-scored encoded narrative-feature space (LLM-extracted features, not text embeddings). Mean distance to own-source centroid and median 10-nearest-neighbor radius. Also centroid distances between sources (human-AI 6.6 vs AI-AI 4.3).

contrasts.reported: Human mean distance to human centroid 22% greater than average AI radius (33.2 vs. 27.4); median 10-nearest-neighbor radius 1.13x larger (33.1 vs. 29.2). Mean human-AI centroid distance 6.6 vs mean AI-AI 4.3.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, Section 5 'AI convergence separates from human narratives'

diversity_detail.metric: Mean Euclidean distance to own-source centroid; median 10-nearest-neighbor radius
diversity_detail.embedding_model: None; z-scored encoded vector of LLM-assigned narrative features (Gemini 3 Flash assignment)
diversity_detail.computed_over: Each story against its source's centroid; each story's 10 nearest neighbors
diversity_detail.notes: Compares diversity of AI-generated vs human-written stories; no person uses AI, so this answers none of the three questions. Number of stories entering this calculation is not stated.

company_involvement.description: Co-author John Wieting is affiliated with Google DeepMind. Acknowledgments thank Google for a Cloud Credit award and Pangram Labs for an OpenRouter credit award.

eligibility.reason: No human participants and no assignment of people to AI assistance. The paper compares stories written by five LLMs with published human stories from Books3 (p. 3), so it is AI-versus-human context evidence. Rarity and dispersion are scored on stories, but not on output that participants produced with or without AI.

one_line_finding: In a parallel corpus of 10,272 Books3 stories and LLM stories from the same prompts, human stories are rarer in narrative-feature space (mean rarity percentile 0.71 vs 0.49 for AI, Cohen's d = 0.83; p. 9, p. 22) and more dispersed (centroid radius 33.2 vs 27.4; p. 9).
open_questions: Test-set size differs between p. 5 (1,384 prompts, 8,301 stories) and Table 12 / Appendix G (8,262 test stories, 1,377 per source); the paper does not explain the gap.
notes: Most of the paper reports human-vs-AI detection and authorship attribution (macro-F1 93.2% binary, 68.4% six-way; Tables 2-3), which are not creativity outcomes and are not listed. The style-edited LAMP test (278 Gemini stories, p. 8) is also detection only.
